concept.name: Fixing
concept.definition: A reference exchange rate determined at a set time each trading day from market transactions and orders around a fixing window, used to value portfolios, settle contracts and execute customer 'fix orders' at a common published price. The most prominent is the London WM/Reuters 4 p.m. fixing in the interbank forex market.
concept.intuition: A fixing is the market's agreed 'official' exchange rate for a given moment each day, so that funds and contracts everywhere can be valued on the same number.
concept.mechanics: A benchmark administrator computes the rate from trades and order-book data captured during a short window around the fixing time (the WM/Reuters 4 p.m. window was widened from one to five minutes in the 2015 reform). Banks accept customer orders guaranteed to execute at the fix price, which concentrates volume into the window; investigations found banks had colluded around the window, leading to penalties and the 2015 reform of the London fixing.
concept.failure_modes: Fixings create manipulation incentives: dealers holding guaranteed fix orders profit by moving the window price, and the 2013-15 FX scandal showed collusive behavior around the London fix. Post-reform, price anomalies around the window and passive execution strategies still generate predictable price patterns.
concept.misconceptions: The fix is not a transaction price anyone can always trade at — it is a computed reference from a short window, and large fix orders are typically executed by dealers over time rather than all at the fix print.
concept.example: An index fund rebalancing at month-end instructs its bank to execute a large currency conversion 'at the 4 p.m. fix'; the bank's execution and hedging flows concentrate into the fixing window.

citations.source: NBER Working Paper 23327 — Did the Reform Fix the London Fix Problem? (Ito and Yamada)
